question.prompt: If the value of the algebraic fraction \((x^2-9)/(x+3)\) is 0, what is the value of \(x\)?

solutions.explanation: For the value to be 0, the numerator must be 0 and the denominator must be nonzero. Solving \(x^2-9=0\) gives \(x=3\) or \(x=-3\). However, when \(x=-3\), the denominator \(x+3=0\), so this value must be discarded. Therefore, \(x=3\).
solutions.title: Find numerator zeros and check the denominator

solutions.explanation:
The denominator requires \(x\ne-3\). Factoring the numerator exposes the same factor as the denominator, so on this domain,
\[
\frac{x^2-9}{x+3}=\frac{(x-3)(x+3)}{x+3}=x-3.
\]
The fraction is therefore 0 exactly when \(x-3=0\), giving \(x=3\), which satisfies the denominator restriction.
solutions.title: Factor and cancel on the original domain
